extracted.intended_audience: writers and screenwriters looking to structure stories using Blake Snyder's Save the Cat! 15-beat framework
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Blake Snyder's 15-beat Save the Cat! story structure (originally for screenplays, widely adapted for fiction) to plan or evaluate a narrative's major story beats and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening Image
rubrics_metrics.description: Snapshot of the protagonist's 'before' world; tone-setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~1% into the story. Serves as a mirror to the Final Image and establishes the protagonist's starting state and story tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme Stated
rubrics_metrics.description: A character (often not the protagonist) hints at the story's deeper meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~5%. Typically a line or moment that signals the central thematic question or lesson the protagonist will confront.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish protagonist, world, status quo, what's missing/broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~1–10%. Introduces main characters, relationships, and the protagonist's ordinary life and flaws; shows what's at stake and what needs to change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalyst
rubrics_metrics.description: The inciting incident; life is disrupted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~10%. A clear event that knocks the protagonist out of the status quo and forces the story question into motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonist hesitates; 'should I or shouldn't I?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~10–20%. The protagonist wrestles with whether to take action; this section dramatizes internal conflict and obstacles to commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Into Two
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonist commits to the new world / quest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~20%. Marks the transition from Act One to Act Two — the protagonist makes a decision that propels them into the main action or the unfamiliar 'new world.'

rubrics_metrics.name: B Story
rubrics_metrics.description: A secondary plot (often love story or mentor) introduced; carries the theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~22%. The B Story supports and reinforces the theme, frequently providing emotional growth or a foil that helps the protagonist internalize the lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fun and Games
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Promise of the premise'; what the genre/title delivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~20–50%. The section where the story delivers on its central premise and genre pleasures — the 'what we came to see' moments, often lighter or exploratory in tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: False victory or false defeat; stakes raised; clock starts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~50%. A pivotal turning point that reframes the story — either a seeming triumph that proves hollow or a crushing setback that forces escalation and urgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad Guys Close In
rubrics_metrics.description: External and internal antagonists ramp up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~50–75%. Antagonistic forces (including the protagonist's inner flaws) tighten their grip, increasing pressure and complications that drive toward crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: All Is Lost
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~75%. The apparent end or worst imaginable outcome where hope seems gone; often marked by a symbolic 'death' moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark Night of the Soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonist absorbs the loss and grows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~75–80%. Quiet, introspective moment following All Is Lost where the protagonist processes failure and discovers the inner change or realization needed to solve the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break Into Three
rubrics_metrics.description: Solution found, often combining A and B stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~80%. The protagonist discovers or commits to a new, integrated approach (often synthesizing lessons from the B Story) and moves into the final act with renewed agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale
rubrics_metrics.description: Five-point finale: gathering team, executing plan, high tower surprise, dig deep down, execution of new plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~80–99%. The climactic sequence where the protagonist assembles allies, implements the plan, faces a major surprise or setback, finds internal reserves ('dig deep'), and ultimately executes a transformed solution that resolves the primary conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Image
rubrics_metrics.description: Mirror of opening image, showing transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position: ~99–100%. A closing snapshot that contrasts with the Opening Image to demonstrate the protagonist's change and the new status quo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snyder's Genre Categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of stories into 10 genres (e.g., Monster in the House, Golden Fleece, Out of the Bottle, Dude with a Problem, Rites of Passage, Buddy Love, Whydunit, The Fool Triumphant, Institutionalized, Superhero) with conventions a story must hit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the genre category to identify and fulfill specific conventions and expectations; each category has characteristic beats and premises that inform how the 'Fun and Games' and other beats play out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save the Cat Moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Early in the story, give the protagonist a moment of likable agency (literally 'saving a cat') so the audience roots for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a scene or small action that humanizes the protagonist and earns audience sympathy, typically placed early (often in the Set-up or Theme Stated area) to secure audience investment even if the protagonist has flaws.
